meta.title: Who really said "I'm not crazy. My reality is just different than yours"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Carroll, and not the Cheshire Cat. Quote Investigator traces it to an anonymous Usenet signature from January 2008.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I'm not crazy. My reality is just different than yours'?
meta.ogDescription: Carroll died in 1898. The earliest known appearance of this line is a 2008 Usenet signature by a poster called Sue.

answer.label: Not Lewis Carroll — an anonymous line from 2008
answer.authorDates: Originator unknown · in circulation since at least January 2008
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator, which has examined this one directly, reports “no substantive evidence supporting the ascription to Lewis Carroll.” The earliest instance it located is a signature block on a Usenet message posted in January 2008 to the newsgroup alt.fiftyplus by someone using the handle Sue — and QI conjectures even she was repeating something already going round, so the originator stays anonymous. The Cheshire Cat picked up the credit in a tweet in March 2011, and Carroll’s own name is attached from January 2012, when a tweet posted the line as “Carroll – Alice in Wonderland”; a padded-out longer wording follows in April 2012. He died in 1898.

source.excerpt: “I’m not crazy, my reality is just different than yours.”
trail: Quote Investigator’s article on this exact saying ↗ is the anchor, and it is unusually blunt: “QI has found no substantive evidence supporting the ascription to Lewis Carroll.” It dates the earliest match to a January 2008 Usenet signature in alt.fiftyplus, then walks the credit forward — a 2009 coffee cup, a 2010 J. C. Penney T-shirt printed with no attribution at all, the Cheshire Cat in March 2011, Carroll in April 2012.

We downloaded the Project Gutenberg texts of ten of Carroll’s English books — 2.41 million characters — Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland ↗ (in two editions), Through the Looking-Glass ↗, The Hunting of the Snark, Phantasmagoria and Other Poems, Three Sunsets and Other Poems, Sylvie and Bruno, Sylvie and Bruno Concluded, A Tangled Tale, The Game of Logic and Symbolic Logic — flattened every line break so no phrase could hide across a line ending, and searched the lot. Neither “my reality” nor “not crazy” occurs once. The line is not a variant of something he wrote; there is nothing there to be a variant of.

We also ran the phrase through a full-text search of the whole of Wikiquote — an insource: query, which reads the raw wikitext of every page on the site. “my reality is just different” returns zero pages. It is not on Carroll’s page ↗, not on the Wonderland page ↗, and not filed anywhere else on the site. That is an absence of a debunk rather than a debunk — but it does mean nobody has found a home for it either.

What Carroll actually wrote about madness is a logic joke, not a slogan. In chapter six of Wonderland ↗ the Cheshire Cat tells Alice a Hatter lives one way and a March Hare the other: “Visit either you like: they’re both mad.” Alice objects that she does not want to go among mad people. “Oh, you can’t help that,” said the Cat: “we’re all mad here. I’m mad. You’re mad.” The Cat then tries to prove its own madness by comparing itself to a dog. That is the register — deadpan and argumentative — and the line on the poster is nothing like it.
source.excerptNote: Quote Investigator’s transcription of the January 2008 Usenet signature — the earliest appearance anyone has found. Note the comma: the full stop that splits the line into two sentences, and the “My” that follows it, are later tidying.

author.name: Lewis Carroll
author.heading: About the name on the graphic
author.bio: Charles Lutwidge Dodgson — Lewis Carroll on the title page — taught mathematics at Christ Church, Oxford for most of his adult life, and wrote the two Alice books and a shelf of logic puzzles alongside it. His real sentences are odd in a particular way: precise, deadpan, and usually about the rules of language rather than about how you feel. That is worth knowing, because the lines invented for him are almost always the opposite — warm, encouraging, and about you.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: Three separate credits have been attached to this line, in the order you would expect: none, then a character, then an author.

items.who: Lewis Carroll, in Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland
items.why: Quote Investigator found no substantive evidence ↗ for it, and the phrase occurs in none of the ten Carroll books we searched. He died in 1898; the earliest trace of the line is from 2008.

The Cat got the credit in a March 2011 tweet, per QI’s chronology ↗ — three years after the line was already circulating with no attribution at all. The Cat’s actual madness lines are in chapter six of Wonderland ↗ and read nothing like it.

items.who: Lewis Carroll — “I’m not strange, weird, off, nor crazy…”
items.why: A padded-out wording that appeared in April 2012 — after the short form had already been credited to Carroll that January — and has since been printed as the Cheshire Cat’s in a 2015 Chicago Tribune column and a 2024 Uncle John’s bathroom reader, both logged by QI ↗. It is later than the short form, not earlier, which is the opposite of what a genuine Victorian original would look like.

misattribution.truthLine: What can be stated flatly: the line is in none of Carroll’s books, and the oldest instance anyone has located is a 2008 forum signature ↗ with no author’s name on it. Who first wrote it is genuinely unknown.

context.heading: Why this one sticks to Carroll
lead: Carroll is a magnet for this kind of line because Wonderland really does have a scene about being mad and not minding — so a reader who half-remembers the Cheshire Cat has somewhere to file a sentence that sounds defiant and slightly pleased with itself. The attribution chain here is visible in the dates: unattributed for three years, then a character, then the author, each step adding authority the line never had.

The J. C. Penney T-shirt is the tell. In August 2010 a department-store advertisement printed the sentence with no author at all — because at that point there was no author to print. The name arrived afterwards, to make a slogan sound like literature.
detailsBody: Quote Investigator’s chronology is worth reading in order: a January 2008 Usenet signature, a May 2008 tweet, a coffee cup in a 2009 role-playing forum, the 2010 T-shirt, a February 2011 tweet still with no attribution, then March 2011 — the Cheshire Cat — and January 2012, “Carroll – Alice in Wonderland”.

By 2015 a Chicago Tribune columnist could write “like Lewis Carroll’s Cheshire Cat” and quote the longer version as though from the book, and by 2024 it had reached a printed quotation collection. None of that adds evidence; it adds repetition, which is a different thing.
context.pull: Unattributed for three years, then a cat, then a Victorian mathematician.

sourcesVerified.claim: QI states there is no substantive evidence for the Lewis Carroll ascription, and dates the earliest located match to a January 2008 Usenet signature in alt.fiftyplus posted by a handle "Sue".
The full text of Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland contains no occurrence of "my reality" or "not crazy"; it does contain the Cheshire Cat’s "we’re all mad here" exchange in chapter six.
The full text of Through the Looking-Glass contains no occurrence of "my reality" or "not crazy".
Carroll's Wikiquote page does not list this line in its sourced or its Misattributed section.
Charles Lutwidge Dodgson (1832-1898), pen name Lewis Carroll, English author and mathematician.
